newsitem.title: USA: US DOE weighs consumer disclosure for electricity.
newsitem.headline: US DOE weighs consumer disclosure for electricity.

text.p: In its recommendations for opening up the U.S. power grid, the Energy Department is considering a consumer disclosure provision on electricity prices and generation sources, a department official said Thursday.

"Consumers would be able to differentiate between offers that are being made by different suppliers" on prices and on the cleanliness of the generation source, Bonnie Suchman, an Energy Department attorney-adviser, said at a panel discussion on power restructuring.
With such a provision, a consumer would have assurance that power advertised as "green" actually was from a clean source, Suchman said.
The department has not released its plans for a restructuring bill, which were being circulated among federal agencies that in some cases have conflicting interests.
The administration must decide whether to push for a federal mandate for retail electricity competition, or for legislation to enable the states to pursue competition.

While Suchman said the federal mandate approach "has a bit of appeal" in providing a uniform system, it also would make stranded costs a federal issue and would make it difficult to take into account different conditions in states when utilities' unrecoverable investments were made.

Suchman also said the administration may call for some sort of "portfolio" requirement to see that use of renewable energy sources called for under existing laws would not be abandoned under deregulation.

She also said the administration was concerned about reliability of the power system in a less regulated environment, and said some kind of self-regulating organization to oversee reliability may be considered.
Electricity deregulation, with its enormous complexity, is expected to move through Congress slowly, although there is more momentum for it in the House of Representatives than the Senate.

Karen Hunsicker, counsel to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, said the committee was weighted even more than usual towards western states, which for the most part have benefited from low rates because of federal dam projects.
"This is not to say they are going to be negative in this issue, but cautious," Hunsicker said.
Several senators from Pacific Northwest states have stressed they would oppose deregulation legislation if it sold off or privatized the Bonneville Power Administration.

Committee Chairman Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, has advocated keeping as much control as possible over deregulation at the state level, which some Senate aides said reduces the chances that Republican senators would back broad federal action.

Northeastern senators also likely would try to block legislation unless they had assurances that their region's air quality would not be hurt in a push for lower-cost power production, said Rich Flick, legislative director for Sen. Dale Bumpers of Arkansas, the ranking Democrat on the Energy Committee.
